title: Paulicians and Bogomils
description: Dualist movements in Armenia and the Balkans, and Byzantium's response

concepts.title: The Paulicians
concepts.contentHtml:
Byzantine writers traced the Paulicians to Constantine of Mananalis, an Armenian who around 660 founded a congregation at Kibossa in eastern Anatolia and took the name Silvanus, after a companion of the apostle Paul. Later leaders also took names from Paul's circle, such as Titus and Timothy. "Paulician" was an outsiders' label; members called themselves simply Christians. Constantine was stoned on imperial orders in the 680s.

Almost everything we know comes from enemies. Peter of Sicily, an imperial envoy who spent months at the Paulician stronghold of Tephrike around 869 to 870, describes two principles: a good heavenly Father who rules the world to come and an evil maker who rules this one. He says Paulicians rejected the Old Testament, refused to honor Mary or the cross, and had no sacraments or priesthood in the Byzantine sense. Nina Garsoïan (The Paulician Heresy, 1967) argued from Armenian sources that the early Paulicians were adoptionists, who saw Jesus as a man adopted as God's Son, and that the dualism belongs to a later phase or to the polemicists' expectations. Others accept a dualist core.

In 843 the empress-regent Theodora ordered the Paulicians to convert or die. Later chroniclers put the dead and dispossessed at 100,000, a figure no one can check. Survivors fled to the Arab emirate of Melitene and, under their leaders Karbeas and then Chrysocheir, built a fortified state around Tephrike (modern Divriği in Turkey) that raided Byzantine Anatolia, reaching Ephesus in 867. Basil I destroyed it in the 870s. Emperors also moved Paulicians west as frontier settlers: Constantine V in 747, and John I Tzimiskes around 970, to the region of Philippopolis, modern Plovdiv in Bulgaria.

concepts.title: Bogomil and the Devil's World
concepts.contentHtml:
In 10th-century Bulgaria, during the reign of Tsar Peter I (927 to 969), a priest called Bogomil began to preach. His name means roughly "dear to God" in Slavonic; his opponent Cosmas punned that he was really "not dear to God." The earliest evidence is a letter from Theophylact, patriarch of Constantinople from 933 to 956, warning the tsar about a new heresy that blended "Manichaeism" with Paulicianism. The fullest early account is the Sermon against the Heretics by the Bulgarian priest Cosmas, probably written soon after 969.

Cosmas says the Bogomils called the visible world the devil's work. They rejected baptism with water, the Eucharist, icons, the cross and church buildings, prayed the Lord's Prayer four times by day and four times by night, avoided meat and wine, and taught people not to obey their masters or the tsar. A later Byzantine account adds a creation myth: Satanael, God's elder son, rebelled, made the material world and shaped Adam's body, and God sent the Word, Christ, to defeat him. Stripped of the divine ending -el, Satanael became plain Satan. This is moderate dualism, in which evil is a fallen power under God, unlike the absolute dualism of two eternal principles held by some later groups.

Bogomil ideas spread into Byzantium, Serbia and Bosnia. A Bulgarian church council under Tsar Boril condemned them in 1211. Whether the medieval Bosnian Church was Bogomil is disputed: older scholarship said yes, while historians such as John Fine argued that it was a schismatic but not dualist church. Westward, a Bogomil text, the Secret Supper (Interrogatio Iohannis), reached Italian Cathars from Bulgaria in the late 12th century.

concepts.title: Basil the Bogomil in Constantinople
concepts.contentHtml:
By the late 11th century Bogomils had followers in Constantinople, and Anna Komnene claims the teaching had reached even the great houses. Her father, the emperor Alexios I Komnenos (r. 1081 to 1118), had a captured Bogomil named Diblatios tortured, and he named the leader: a monk and physician called Basil, who had chosen twelve disciples as his "apostles." Anna tells the story in the Alexiad, written in the 1140s, a source that admires her father without reserve.

Alexios invited Basil to the palace, shared his table and posed as a would-be disciple. Basil set out his teaching while a secretary hidden behind a curtain wrote it down. Then the curtain was drawn back before the assembled senate, army commanders and clergy. Basil refused to recant. Suspects were sorted by a test: two pyres were lit, one with a cross fixed beside it, and the accused were told to choose. Those who walked toward the cross were released as Orthodox; the rest went back to prison, where some later recanted and others died. Basil himself, condemned by the patriarch and synod, was burned on a great pyre in the Hippodrome after one last offer of pardon.

The dates are disputed. Basil's interrogation is usually placed around 1100, but Anna's narrative is out of order, and historians have dated the burning anywhere from about 1100 to as late as 1117 or 1118. Alexios also commissioned the theologian Euthymios Zigabenos to write up Bogomil doctrine, drawing on Basil's statements, for his Dogmatic Panoply. That account is the main source for the Satanael myth and the fullest systematic description of Bogomil belief that survives.

title: The Cathars
description: Good men, believers, a crusade, the Inquisition and an argument about invention

concepts.title: Good Men, Believers and the Consolamentum
concepts.contentHtml:
From the mid-12th century Catholic writers reported organized dualist heretics in the Rhineland, northern Italy and Languedoc in southern France. In sermons of 1163 the Rhineland monk Eckbert of Schönau called them Cathars, Cathari, from Greek katharoi, "pure ones"; others called them Albigensians, after the town of Albi. Neither was a self-name. In Languedoc, people called their holy men and women "good men" and "good women" (bons omes) or "good Christians."

According to the sources, the core teaching was dualist: the visible world of matter was the work of an evil power, and human souls were spirits trapped in bodies, passing from body to body until released. Some Cathars, especially in Italy, held absolute dualism, two eternal principles; others held a moderate form like the Bogomils'. The church had two tiers. The good men and women, whom inquisitors called perfecti, meaning fully fledged heretics rather than morally perfect people, lived celibate lives, owned little, prayed often and ate no meat, eggs or cheese, though fish was allowed. Ordinary credentes, believers, married, worked and greeted the good men with a ritual bow and request for blessing, the melioramentum.

The one rite that mattered was the consolamentum, a spiritual baptism by the laying on of hands, with the Gospel of John held over the head. It made a believer one of the good Christians. Most believers put it off until their deathbed, since sinning afterward would undo it. Cathar rituals in Latin and Occitan, and an Italian treatise, the Book of the Two Principles, survive in the movement's own words.

concepts.title: The Albigensian Crusade
concepts.contentHtml:
In January 1208 the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau was murdered near Saint-Gilles on the Rhône. Pope Innocent III blamed Count Raymond VI of Toulouse, long accused of sheltering heretics, and called a crusade against the heretics of Languedoc, offering the same spiritual rewards as an expedition to the Holy Land. In the summer of 1209 a northern French army, guided by the legate Arnaud Amaury, abbot of Cîteaux, reached Béziers. On 22 July the city fell and much of its population was killed, including people who had taken refuge in churches.

Arnaud's own report to the pope said that nearly 20,000 died, sparing neither rank, sex nor age. Historians treat the number as an exaggeration, but the massacre was real. The famous line "Kill them all; God will know his own" (Caedite eos. Novit enim Dominus qui sunt eius) first appears in the Dialogue on Miracles of the German Cistercian Caesarius of Heisterbach, written around 1219 to 1223. Caesarius says only that Arnaud "is said to have" spoken it, and many historians doubt that he did.

Carcassonne surrendered in August 1209, and military leadership passed to Simon de Montfort. Mass burnings followed: about 140 good men and women at Minerve in 1210, and around 400 at Lavaur in 1211, by one chronicler's count. King Peter II of Aragon, who came to defend his vassals, was killed at Muret in 1213. Simon died besieging Toulouse in 1218, struck by a stone from a siege engine. The French crown took over the war in 1226, and the Treaty of Paris in 1229 bound Languedoc to France.

concepts.title: Montségur and the Invention Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
The crusade did not end the good men. The Council of Toulouse in 1229 ordered systematic searches, and from 1233 Pope Gregory IX entrusted inquiries into heresy to Dominican friars. Inquisitors questioned whole villages and wrote down the answers, creating the archive historians still use. In May 1242 a band from the mountain castle of Montségur killed two inquisitors and their party at Avignonet. A royal army besieged Montségur from May 1243. The defenders agreed terms in early March 1244, and on 16 March more than 200 good men and women who would not renounce their faith, were burned below the castle. The last known good man in Languedoc, Guillaume Bélibaste, was burned in 1321.

A long debate asks how far "Catharism" was the persecutors' creation. R. I. Moore (The Formation of a Persecuting Society, 1987; The War on Heresy, 2012) argued that the medieval church largely constructed the heresy it pursued, as part of building its own authority. Mark Gregory Pegg (The Corruption of Angels, 2001) argued that Languedoc had no organized dualist church: the good men were local holy people, and the tidy dualist system came from clerics who read ancient heresies into them.

Other historians, among them Peter Biller, Bernard Hamilton and Claire Taylor, reply that the movement's own texts, Italian evidence such as the treatise of the former Cathar turned inquisitor Rainier Sacconi (1250), and links with Balkan dualists show a real, if varied, dualist church. The essays in Cathars in Question (2016), edited by Antonio Sennis, set out both sides. Most now accept that inquisitors' categories shaped the record, while disagreeing about how much lay beneath them.

title: The Church of the East
description: From Persia to China: the church misnamed Nestorian

concepts.title: Nestorius, Ephesus and a Misleading Name
concepts.contentHtml:
Nestorius, a monk of Antioch, became bishop of Constantinople in 428. He objected to calling Mary Theotokos, "God-bearer," because it seemed to blur the human and the divine in Christ, and suggested Christotokos, "Christ-bearer." Cyril of Alexandria accused him of splitting Christ into two persons. At the Council of Ephesus in 431, Cyril opened proceedings before the bishops from Antioch arrived and had Nestorius deposed; the Antiochenes then held their own council and deposed Cyril. The emperor Theodosius II upheld Nestorius's removal and in 435 exiled him to the Great Oasis in Egypt, where he died around 451. His defense, the Bazaar of Heracleides, survives only in Syriac.

The church later called "Nestorian" was not founded by him. Christianity had reached Persia, outside the Roman Empire, by the 3rd century at the latest. In 410 a synod at the Sasanian capital, Seleucia-Ctesiphon, organized its bishops under a catholicos, and in 424 they declared that bishops in the Roman west could not judge them. When the emperor Zeno closed the school of Edessa in 489, its teachers moved to Nisibis in Persia. The church adopted the theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia, whose ideas Nestorius had followed, and Babai the Great (died 628) gave it a classic form: two natures and two qnome in one person.

The church honors Nestorius as a teacher but did not call itself Nestorian; it is the Church of the East, today chiefly the Assyrian Church of the East. Sebastian Brock called the label "a lamentable misnomer" in 1996. In 1994 Pope John Paul II and Patriarch Mar Dinkha IV signed a joint declaration agreeing that their two ways of speaking about Christ express the same faith.

concepts.title: Across Asia to Chang'an
concepts.contentHtml:
From Mesopotamia the church followed the trade routes east. By the 5th century it had bishops at Merv and Herat in Central Asia, and Sogdian merchants carried it toward Samarkand and beyond. Patriarch Timothy I (780 to 823), who debated the caliph al-Mahdi in Baghdad, consecrated metropolitans for the Turks and for China. Between the 9th and 14th centuries the Church of the East spread over more territory than any other Christian body, with 20 to 30 metropolitan provinces by the 10th century.

In 781 a stone stele nearly 3 meters tall was set up in or near Chang'an, the Tang capital and modern Xi'an. Its Chinese inscription, with names and notes in Syriac, was composed by a monk named Jingjing, in Syriac Adam. It records that a missionary called Aluoben (Alopen) arrived from the west in 635 and was received by Emperor Taizong, who allowed his teaching. The stele calls it Jingjiao, the "Luminous Religion," and explains creation, the fall and the incarnation partly in Buddhist and Daoist vocabulary. It lists dozens of clergy by name.

The Xi'an Stele was probably buried during the persecution of 845, when Emperor Wuzong turned on Buddhism and foreign religions, and was dug up again between about 1621 and 1625. Jesuits publicized it in Europe; some 18th-century skeptics, Voltaire among them, called it a forgery, but it is accepted as genuine and stands in the Forest of Steles museum in Xi'an. Christian texts of the Tang period also survived in the sealed library cave at Dunhuang. In 987 a monk back from China told the Baghdad writer Ibn al-Nadim that Christianity there had all but died out.

concepts.title: The Mongol Revival and Rabban Bar Sauma
concepts.contentHtml:
The church revived under the Mongols. Several steppe peoples, among them the Keraits, Naimans and Önggüt, had Christian rulers or large Christian communities. Sorghaghtani Beki, a Kerait Christian princess, was the mother of the Great Khans Möngke and Kublai and of Hülegü, founder of the Ilkhanate in Persia, whose chief wife Doquz Khatun was also a Christian. Under Kublai's Yuan dynasty, Christians, known as Yelikewen, had their own government office, and new metropolitan provinces were created in north China.

Rabban Bar Sauma, born around 1220 near Khanbaliq (Beijing), was a monk of Uyghur or Önggüt origin. In the 1270s he and his younger disciple Markos set out for Jerusalem. War stopped them short, and in 1281 Markos was elected patriarch as Yahballaha III. In 1287 the Ilkhan Arghun sent Bar Sauma west to seek an alliance against the Mamluks of Egypt. He met the Byzantine emperor Andronikos II in Constantinople, saw Etna erupt, found the papacy vacant in Rome and discussed doctrine with the cardinals, wintered in Genoa, spent about a month with Philip IV in Paris, and met Edward I of England in Gascony. Back in Rome in 1288, the new pope, Nicholas IV, gave him communion on Palm Sunday.

No alliance followed. Bar Sauma died in Baghdad in 1294; his journey is known from a Syriac history of him and Yahballaha that draws on his own account. The Ilkhan Ghazan's conversion to Islam in 1295, the fall of the Yuan in 1368 and Timur's campaigns late in the 14th century shattered the church. Its remnants survived mainly in northern Mesopotamia and the Hakkari mountains.

title: St Thomas Christians of India
description: An apostolic tradition, a Syriac church in Kerala and a Portuguese rupture

concepts.title: The Thomas Tradition and Its Evidence
concepts.contentHtml:
The Christians of Kerala, on India's southwest coast, trace their church to the apostle Thomas. Their tradition says he landed at Muziris, near modern Kodungallur, in 52 CE, founded seven churches along the coast and was killed at Mylapore, now part of Chennai, traditionally in 72 CE. Songs and family histories carry the story; one, the Thomma Parvam, was written down in 1601.

The earliest written link between Thomas and India is the Acts of Thomas, a Syriac work of the early 3rd century, probably from Edessa. It sends Thomas to the court of a king named Gudnaphar. That detail once looked like pure romance, but coins and an inscription from Takht-i-Bahi in present-day Pakistan show that an Indo-Parthian king called Gondophares ruled in the northwest in the first half of the 1st century CE. The Acts place Thomas in the northwest, not Kerala, and their story is legendary in style. By the 4th century Ephrem the Syrian wrote that Thomas's bones had been brought from India to Edessa.

A voyage to Kerala in the 1st century was possible: Roman ships traded for pepper at Muziris, and excavations at Pattanam since 2007 have turned up Roman amphorae. Possible is not proven. No 1st-century evidence places Thomas in India, and historians divide between those who think the tradition may keep a real memory and those who see a later claim. A second tradition tells of Thomas of Cana, a Syrian merchant who brought Christian families from Mesopotamia in the 4th century or, by another dating, the 8th; the Knanaya community traces its descent from them.

concepts.title: A Syriac Church in Malabar
concepts.contentHtml:
Whatever its origin, by late antiquity Kerala's church was tied to the Church of the East. Around 550 the Alexandrian traveler Cosmas Indicopleustes reported Christians in Taprobane (Sri Lanka) and in Male, "where the pepper grows," and a bishop appointed from Persia at a place called Kalliana. For roughly a thousand years Kerala's bishops came from Mesopotamia. Patriarch Timothy I made India a metropolitan province, and an Indian archdeacon, drawn from local priestly families, handled day-to-day leadership.

The liturgy was in East Syriac, the church language of the Church of the East, while daily life was in Malayalam. The Tharisapalli copper plates of Kollam, dated to about 849, record a local ruler under the Chera king Sthanu Ravi granting land, privileges and serfs to a church built by the Syrian Christian merchant Mar Sapir Iso. Witnesses signed in Arabic, Middle Persian and Judeo-Persian, a snapshot of a cosmopolitan pepper port. Stone crosses carved with Middle Persian inscriptions, the so-called Persian crosses, survive at St Thomas Mount in Chennai and at Kottayam.

The Thomas Christians held a respected place in Kerala society, with trading privileges and customs of dress, house building and marriage close to those of high-caste Hindu neighbors. They were often called Nasranis, from "Nazarenes." This combination, Syriac in worship, Indian in culture and loyal to a distant patriarch in Mesopotamia, is what the Portuguese found when Vasco da Gama reached the coast in 1498.

concepts.title: Diamper and the Bent Cross
concepts.contentHtml:
The Portuguese first welcomed fellow Christians, then judged them Nestorian heretics. When the last East Syriac metropolitan, Mar Abraham, died in 1597, Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes of Goa moved to bring the church under Rome and Portuguese patronage. He convened the Synod of Diamper (Udayamperur), near Kochi, from 20 to 26 June 1599. Its roughly 200 decrees condemned Nestorius and the Patriarch of Babylon, purged the Syriac liturgy of passages judged heretical, ordered suspect Syriac books handed over for burning, imposed clerical celibacy and banned many local customs. A Jesuit, Francisco Ros, became bishop. Historians question the synod's legitimacy, since Menezes had no ordinary authority there, and some Syriac texts survived by concealment.

Resentment grew. In 1652 a Syriac bishop from the Middle East named Ahatallah reached India, was seized by the Portuguese and shipped away. Rumor said he had been drowned; more likely he was handed to the Inquisition and died in Europe. On 3 January 1653 a crowd at Mattancherry, near Kochi, held ropes tied to a stone cross and swore not to submit to the Jesuits or the Portuguese. The cross is said to have bent under the strain, hence the Coonan Cross Oath, the oath of the bent cross. The exact wording, and whether it rejected Rome itself, is disputed.

The community split. Rome sent Carmelites, who by 1663 had won back 84 of 116 churches; their heirs include the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church. Others followed Archdeacon Thomas, consecrated by twelve priests as Mar Thoma I, and in 1665 a bishop from the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate began introducing West Syriac worship. Several churches, Catholic, Orthodox, Mar Thoma and Assyrian, now descend from the one community.

title: Ethiopia's Distinctive Christianity
description: Ge'ez, a larger Bible, the Ark at Aksum and a demanding calendar of fasts

concepts.title: Aksum, Alexandria and Ge'ez
concepts.contentHtml:
Christianity became the faith of Aksum's court in the 4th century, when King Ezana turned from the old gods to the "Lord of Heaven" (see the African Kingdoms topic). According to the church historian Rufinus, writing around 400, a young Christian from Tyre named Frumentius, brought to Aksum as a captive, rose at court and was later consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria. Ethiopians remember him as Abba Salama. The tie to Alexandria lasted sixteen centuries: the church's head, the abun, was an Egyptian monk sent by the Coptic patriarch until the Ethiopian church became self-governing in 1959, with Abuna Basilios as its first patriarch.

Like the Coptic, Armenian and Syriac Orthodox churches, the Ethiopian church rejected the Council of Chalcedon of 451, which defined Christ as one person in two natures. Its full name, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, uses the Ge'ez word tewahedo, "made one," for the single united nature of the incarnate Christ. Tradition credits the Nine Saints, monks who arrived in the late 5th century, with spreading monasticism and translating scripture; the old view that they came from Syria is now doubted.

Ge'ez, a Semitic language, was the speech of Aksum. Its script grew from the South Arabian alphabet, and in the 4th century scribes began marking vowels on each consonant, creating the syllabic fidel still used for Amharic and Tigrinya. Ge'ez probably stopped being an everyday spoken language somewhere between the 10th and 13th centuries, but it remains the language of worship. The Garima Gospels, kept at the monastery of Abba Garima, are among the oldest illuminated Christian manuscripts; radiocarbon dating puts the older volume around 390 to 570.

concepts.title: A Bigger Bible
concepts.contentHtml:
The Ethiopian Bible is the largest of any church. Its traditional count is 81 books, although lists differ on which books make up that number. It keeps works that other churches set aside. Two stand out. 1 Enoch, in Ge'ez Henok, is a collection of Jewish apocalyptic writings from about the 3rd century BCE to around the 1st century CE. It tells of the Watchers, fallen angels who taught forbidden arts and fathered giants, and of Enoch's journeys through the heavens. Jubilees, in Ge'ez Kufale, retells Genesis and the start of Exodus as a revelation to Moses on Sinai, dividing history into 49-year jubilee periods and following a 364-day solar calendar.

Both books were known to early Christians: the New Testament Letter of Jude (verses 14 to 15) quotes 1 Enoch as prophecy. In the Greek and Latin churches they fell out of use and were later known only in fragments. Ethiopia preserved them complete. The Scottish traveler James Bruce brought copies of 1 Enoch to Europe in 1773, and Richard Laurence published an English translation in 1821. When the Dead Sea Scrolls came to light after 1947, Aramaic fragments of Enoch and Hebrew fragments of Jubilees from Qumran confirmed that the Ge'ez texts descend from ancient Jewish originals.

The Ethiopian Old Testament also includes three books of Meqabyan, which despite the name are unrelated to the Greek books of Maccabees, and the Paralipomena of Jeremiah, sometimes called 4 Baruch. A broader New Testament adds church-order books such as the Sinodos and the Book of the Covenant. Scholars speak of a narrower and a broader canon, and no single council ever fixed its edges.

concepts.title: Ark, Tabot and Fast
concepts.contentHtml:
Ethiopian tradition holds that the Ark of the Covenant rests at Aksum, in a chapel beside the Church of St Mary of Zion. The full story is told in the 14th-century Kebra Nagast (see the African Kingdoms topic): Menelik, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought the Ark from Jerusalem. One monk, appointed for life, guards it, and no one else may see it. Outsiders have never examined the claim. The scholar Edward Ullendorff said in 1992 that he had been shown the object in 1941 and found an empty wooden box of medieval workmanship; his account cannot be checked either.

The Ark matters in every parish. Each church holds a tabot, a consecrated tablet of wood or stone representing the Ark and the tablets of the Law, kept in an inner sanctuary only priests may enter. It is the tabot, not the building, that is consecrated. At Timkat, the feast of Christ's baptism on 19 January (20 January in some years), priests carry the cloth-wrapped tabots in procession to water.

Fasting is the most demanding practice: about 250 fast days a year, of which roughly 180 bind lay people. On fast days believers avoid all animal products and traditionally eat nothing until midday or later; Lent lasts 55 days. The church also keeps Saturday as a Sabbath beside Sunday, a practice championed by the monk Ewostatewos and accepted at a council under Emperor Zara Yaqob in 1450, and it practices male circumcision and Old Testament food laws. Ullendorff (1956) read such customs as traces of ancient Jewish influence; critics such as Maxime Rodinson argued that a church reading the Old Testament closely could have adopted them later.

title: Hidden and Surviving Minorities
description: Hussites, Moravians, Mozarabs and what it means for a Christianity to be lost

concepts.title: Hussites and Moravians
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1415 the Council of Constance burned the Prague preacher Jan Hus as a heretic, despite a safe-conduct from King Sigismund. Bohemia rose. In the Four Articles of Prague (1420) the Hussites demanded free preaching, communion in both bread and wine for lay people, a church stripped of worldly wealth and the punishment of public sin. The chalice became their symbol. Between 1420 and 1431 they defeated five crusades under commanders such as Jan Žižka. After moderate Hussites and Catholic nobles crushed the radicals at Lipany in 1434, the Compacts of Basel (1436) let Bohemia keep communion in both kinds, and a separate Utraquist church lasted about two centuries.

From the Hussite world came the Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum), founded around 1457 at Kunvald. In its early years it rejected oaths and violence and stressed discipline and simple living. After the Protestant defeat at White Mountain in 1620, the Habsburgs re-Catholicized Bohemia and Moravia. The Brethren's last bishop, the educator Jan Amos Comenius, died in exile in 1670, praying for a "hidden seed" left behind. Secret Protestants did survive until Joseph II's Patent of Toleration in 1781, which recognized only Lutherans and Reformed, not the Brethren.

In 1722 refugees from Moravia settled on the Saxon estate of Count Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf and built Herrnhut. A renewal on 13 August 1727 launched the Moravian Church, which kept a round-the-clock prayer watch for about a century and from 1732 sent missionaries abroad, starting with the Danish Caribbean island of St Thomas. Moravians helped shape John Wesley's conversion experience in 1738, and the church now has over a million members, many of them in Tanzania.

concepts.title: The Mozarabs of al-Andalus
concepts.contentHtml:
After the Muslim conquest of Iberia began in 711, many of the peninsula's Christians lived under Islamic rule as protected but subordinate dhimmis, paying a special tax. Christian sources from the 11th century on called them Mozarabs, from Arabic musta'rib, "Arabized"; Muslims did not use the term. Many spoke a Romance dialect at home and Arabic in public. In 854 the Córdoban layman Paulus Alvarus complained that young Christians delighted in Arabic poetry and wrote Arabic elegantly, yet hardly one in a thousand could write a decent Latin letter.

Between 850 and 859, 48 Christians in Córdoba, many of them monks and nuns, were executed, most for publicly denouncing Islam or for apostasy. The priest Eulogius, who wrote their stories and was himself beheaded in 859, praised them as martyrs. Many local Christians saw the provocations as reckless, and a council of bishops called under the emir in 852 discouraged seeking martyrdom. Under the Almoravids in the 12th century, many Mozarabs fled north, and in 1126 large numbers were deported to North Africa.

Their liturgy outlived them. The Hispanic or Mozarabic rite, the native liturgy of Visigothic Spain, was set aside in Castile after the Council of Burgos in 1080, under pressure from Pope Gregory VII and King Alfonso VI. When Alfonso took Toledo in 1085, he let six parishes keep it. A legend says the two missals were tested by fire. In 1500 and 1502 Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros printed the Mozarabic missal and breviary and endowed a chapel in Toledo Cathedral, where the rite is still celebrated daily. Revised books appeared from 1988, and Pope John Paul II celebrated the rite in 1992.

concepts.title: What "Lost" Really Means
concepts.contentHtml:
"Lost" covers very different fates. Some movements were destroyed. After Guillaume Bélibaste's burning in 1321 no Cathar good man is known in Languedoc; the "Cathar country" of modern tourism is a reinvention. Nubia's Christian kingdoms along the Nile, Christian from the 6th century, faded between the 14th and 16th centuries. Murals from the cathedral of Faras, rescued by Polish archaeologists in the 1960s before Lake Nasser flooded the site, are now in Warsaw and Khartoum.

Others were absorbed. Many Paulicians in Bulgaria became Catholics in the 16th and 17th centuries. After the failed Chiprovtsi uprising of 1688 some fled across the Danube and became the Banat Bulgarians, and the town of Pavlikeni is generally thought to keep their name. Some survived in hiding, like Bohemia's "hidden seed" and Japan's Kakure Kirishitan, who kept Christian prayers without priests for about 250 years (covered in Mysteries and Hidden Faiths). Some simply shrank. In the Chüy Valley of Kyrgyzstan, gravestones of a Church of the East community dated 1338 to 1339 mention a pestilence, and a 2022 ancient DNA study found plague bacteria in people buried there, close to the ancestor of the strains of the Black Death.

And some were never lost except from a Western viewpoint. The Assyrian Church of the East, the Thomas Christians and the Ethiopian church are living churches, with tens of millions of members between them. Philip Jenkins's The Lost History of Christianity (2008) argued that for about a thousand years Christianity's heartlands lay as much in the Middle East, Africa and Asia as in Europe. Bart Ehrman's Lost Christianities (2003) uses the phrase for the varied Christian groups of the 2nd century, a different story.
